implementation_notes: Ruby's standard library ships the delegation machinery, so the envelope's forwarding is generated rather than written: `extend Forwardable` plus `def_delegators :@letter, :draw, :size` defines one forwarding method per name, and `DelegateClass(Letter)` or SimpleDelegator builds a whole envelope class around a letter - SimpleDelegator additionally exposes __setobj__, which is exactly the 'swap the letter at run time' variant of the idiom. Hand-written forwarding is still justified when the envelope must publish a deliberate, documented subset of the letter's API instead of a list of method names, or when the calls need interception. Note that both modules must be required explicitly; they are stdlib, not core.
code_sketch:
require "forwardable"
require "delegate"

class Envelope
  extend Forwardable
  def_delegators :@letter, :draw, :size      # stdlib writes the forwarders
  def initialize(letter) = @letter = letter
end

swappable = SimpleDelegator.new(letter)      # envelope with a replaceable letter
swappable.__setobj__(other_letter)
pitfalls: def_delegators forwards only the names listed, and method_missing-based delegation (SimpleDelegator) forwards everything - including methods whose signature or meaning changed - so mistakes surface at call time.
DelegateClass creates a new class on every call; build it once (or use SimpleDelegator) instead of inside a loop or a factory that runs per request.

SimpleDelegator fixes its method set from the first delegate: __setobj__ keeps the old methods, so swapping in an object of a different type silently changes nothing (the documentation warns against it).
